newsitem.title: FRANCE: French, German ex-leaders call for weak currencies.
newsitem.headline: French, German ex-leaders call for weak currencies.

text.p: Former leaders of France and Germany renewed their offensives against the current architects of a planned European single currency on Friday and called for a weaker franc and mark.

Former German Chancellor Helmut Schmidt and former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing said in separate newspaper interviews adherance to strong currencies by France and Germany was damaging growth and new solutions needed to be found to reduce unemployment.

Schmidt said he agreed with Giscard d'Estaing that both the franc and the mark were overvalued and said the Bundesbank's monetary policy had been largely responsible for the rise in unemployment in Germany during the past twenty years.

"The consequences of the strong mark ideology can be seen in a simple difference: In Germany, where unemployment is over 10 percent, the discount rate at which banks refinance themselves at the central bank is 2.5 percent. In Japan, where unemployment is half as high, the central bank's money costs 0.5 percent," Schmidt said in the French daily Liberation.
"The government has itself to blame if all it has done for the last two years is talk constantly about the stability of the mark and done nothing to cut unemployment," he was reported as saying.

He said the concept of a stable or solid euro and mark was full of misunderstandings as the mark has been far from stable during the past 25 years. He said the rise in the value of the mark was chiefly the result of Bundesbank policy and that it had seriously damaged the competitivity of German goods.
Bundesbank policy "shares a large part of the responsibility for the unemployment that's appeared in Germany during the last twenty years," said Schmidt.
Giscard was equally critical of the current French government's refusal to consider re-evaluating the level of the franc in 1995 to try and reduce unemployment.

"The day after the presidential election I thought there were two urgent economic measures that needed to be taken: a reduction in the payroll charges and the setting of the level of the franc," Giscard said in the financial daily La Tribune.
"It was necessary then to foster the decline in unemployment which started in the first half of 1995," he said.

Giscard said the franc, currently at 5.26 against the dollar, should be around 5.50 to 5.60 and that the French currency should be at 3.50 against the German mark when converted into euros, compared with 3.38 now.

Giscard d'Estaing, who has repeatedly called for a weaker currency and greater efforts to spur growth at a time when Paris is cutting spending to prepare for monetary union, also said the Bank of France had room to cut interest rates independently of the Bundesbank and that the French central banks's five basis point cut earlier this week had been "timid".

Schmidt also said he thought some Bundesbank officials were trying to sabotage the planned move to a single European currency in 1999 and that the German government had been wrong to try and insist on a strict pact for imposing fiscal discipline on members of the euro bloc.
"The gentlemen of the Bundesbank believe that a single currency must be made on their terms or not at all," Schmidt said.

"I continue to believe that the officials of the Bundesbank are campaigning against a single currency. Not all of them. But certainly (chief economist Otmar) Issing or (president Hans) Tietmeyer," Schmidt said.

Asked if he was grateful for French insistence on softening the terms of the so-called "stability pact" he said German Finance Minister Theo Waigel had been wrong to take such a strict position on the pact.

"It is not that it was 'softened', the German position was absolutely not imposed. The French were right and reason carried the day. The German finance minister and the Bundesbank were mistaken about Germany's true interests," he said.
